title: Working from a café
summary_es: Trabajar desde una cafetería: ventajas, quejas y normas no escritas. Expresiones fijas y verbos con preposición.
text: More and more people now choose to work from cafés rather than from home or an office. At first {{1}}, the idea seems odd: cafés are noisy, the wifi is unreliable and the chairs are rarely comfortable. Yet research suggests that a moderate level of background noise can actually {{2}} creativity. There is also a social side. Even if you never {{3}} a word with the people around you, simply being among others who are busy can make it easier to {{4}} on your own work. Not everyone is convinced. Café owners complain that some customers {{5}} a table for hours after buying a single coffee, and several cafés have {{6}} time limits or switched off the wifi at lunchtime. Regular remote workers say the solution is simple: order something every hour or so, {{7}} your voice down during calls and, above all, do not {{8}} it for granted that the table is yours for the day.

gaps.explanation_es: Expresión fija: «at first sight» = a primera vista.
«Boost» = potenciar, dar un empujón a algo (creativity, sales, confidence). «Rise» no lleva complemento, y «enlarge» y «extend» son para tamaño o duración.
«Exchange a word with someone» = cruzar una palabra con alguien.
«Concentrate on». Las otras van con to: attend to, devote yourself to, pay attention to.
Una mesa se «ocupa» (occupy a table). «Spend» y «pass» van con tiempo, y «last» no lleva complemento.
«Introduce a rule / a limit» = implantar una norma. Es la colocación habitual para medidas nuevas.
«Take it for granted that…» = dar por hecho que…
